Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian has said that it is now time to end the war between Tehran and the US on Friday. "It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity," Pezeshkian said in a meeting with doctors in the country.
US military presence in Middle East could be cut back after Iran war ends: report
The Pentagon is considering reducing US military presence in the Middle East following the conclusion of the Iran war, according to a report.
Troops could be withdrawn from the Persian Gulf, officials told The Washington Post, following months of attacks by Iranian forces that have targeted US bases across the region since the war began in late February.
The Pentagon’s policy office is evaluating US regional presence, with US Central Command (Centcom) and Joint Staff also looking at the situation, a senior Pentagon official told the outlet.
More here.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/06/23/17/22/FILES-QATAR-US-IRAQ-UDEID-AIR-BASE-ctzbeasu.jpeg?trim=2,0,3,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
Here’s why Gaza peace deals keep unravelling
Donald Trump’s Board of Peace published a 15-point roadmap for Gaza in late July in which Hamas would hand its weapons to a committee of Palestinian technocrats, certified by an international verification body, and Israel would withdraw from the strip in phases.
After Israel officially rejected the plan on August 9, US envoy Jared Kushner flew to the Egyptian coast to meet Hamas representatives.
From there, he travelled to Jerusalem where it was proposed the weapons would instead be handed over under the supervision of an American general. This change to the disarmament process is a clear illustration of what has gone wrong with each agreement reached over Gaza since January 2025: none have established, in advance, who certifies compliance.
More here.
Iran says Trump's sanctions 'assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty'
Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said this morning that the imminent US announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran was an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations".
"Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law," he said in a post on X.
US president Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides "any type of lifeline to Iran," said yesterday that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict.
Iran asks Qatar to transfer 'detained pilots' to hospital on land
Iran has claimed that Qatar was holding its pilots captive in "poor physical condition" on water.
Iranian officials have called on Qatar to transfer the detained pilots to a hospital on land, according to the Tasnim news agency.
Qatar on Tuesday said that an Iranian delegation travelled to Doha and collected the remains of one of its pilots.
However, Tehran has claimed that three pilots who went missing after their aircraft entered Qatari airspace and were shot down in March were still in the country.
Pentagon says more than 750 US troops wounded and 18 killed in Iran war
The Pentagon says 756 US service members have been wounded and 18 killed in the war against Iran since late February, bringing total US military casualties to 774.
The figures, per the Defence Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) data, were updated after the Pentagon added 50 wounded personnel to its casualty database.
The update comes amid renewed US strikes on Iran, stalled efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and US president Donald Trump’s announcement of a major new economic campaign against Iran.
Iran grants Iraq permission for its oil tankers to pass through Hormuz
Iran has agreed to allow some Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, after Iraqi parliament speaker Haibat al-Halbousi requested special permission from his Iranian counterpart Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
According to Iran’s official IRNA news agency, the move is aimed at protecting Iraq’s oil exports and economic interests, but Iran has not said how many tankers will be allowed through or for how long.
Reza Pahlavi condemns Iran fuel price hikes
Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last shah, has criticised the government’s proposed fuel price increases, calling them an “unforgivable mistake” that would worsen hardship for Iranians.
In a post on X, Pahlavi wrote: “While the Islamic Republic squanders the nation's resources on foreign terrorists and domestic oppressors, the regime's officials and their cronies compete with one another in plundering national wealth, and the regime's ineptitude in governing the country has broken the backs of households and impoverished Iranians. Imposing fuel price hikes on the people is an unforgivable mistake and a profound betrayal. Fuel prices cannot be compared to those in other countries when Iranians' incomes are in rials and below the poverty line.
“Fuel and energy issues are managed on a daily basis without crisis in nearly every country in the world, even many with far fewer resources than Iran.”
He continued: “On one hand, the IRGC smuggling mafia siphons off tens of millions of litres of Iran's capital daily through tankers, pipelines, and smuggling docks; on the other, the automotive mafia foists low-quality, high-consumption vehicles on the nation. This criminal sect, incapable of solving the problem, uses its propaganda apparatus to shift the burden of fuel shortages onto the people, portraying them as the cause of increased consumption and fuel smuggling.
“The Islamic Republic is an incompetent, corrupt, and anti-Iranian regime that is itself the root of these disorders and will never be capable of resolving them.”
Iran army warns of ‘broader’ response to any attack
Iran’s military has adopted a more “offensive” approach from a “defensive” one following the experience of recent wars, army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia said, according to Iranian state media.
Akraminia said: “Our country’s military doctrine was defensive in the past, but gradually during these two wars, we witnessed the military doctrine moving from a defensive posture towards an offensive one.”
He said that the change “does not mean carrying out preemptive operations against the enemy.
“We will respond to any act of aggression immediately and on a broader scale than the aggression itself.”
According to Akraminia, Iran has restored military equipment damaged in previous fighting and brought additional systems into operation. “We are working continuously so that if the enemy again makes a miscalculation, we can deliver a more crushing response than before,” he said.
Akraminia also said Iran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz had become a “decisive geopolitical influence” following the war, while pointing to a new Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani defence partnership as evidence of what he described as waning US influence in the region.
Israel faces backlash over building of gallows site for hanging Palestinians
Israel’s far-right national security minister is facing a major backlash over the construction of a gallows site to execute Palestinians sentenced to death at a prison in Israel.
Itamar Ben-Gvir posted a video online showing the construction of the facility in an unidentified location, which will include viewing booths for the family members of victims to witness executions.
It follows the passage of a highly controversial “Death Penalty for Terrorists Law” earlier this year that made death by hanging a default sentence for Palestinians convicted in military courts of deadly attacks.
More here.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/09/22/7/20/SEI264491737.jpg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
US energy secretary says 'oil flowing through Hormuz'
US energy secretary Chris Wright has claimed that the US military has helped transit more than 15 million barrels of oil out of Hormuz on Tuesday.
"Combined with pipelines, the total oil leaving the region was close to 20 million barrels," he said on X.
He added: "Make no mistake, thanks to the US Navy, oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. The seven-day average of oil leaving the Strait is over 8 million barrels a day."
summary: US President Donald Trump claimed that Iran is not yet ready to make the right deal as tensions persist between the two nations. Meanwhile, the Pentagon reported that US military casualties in the conflict have risen to 18 killed and 756 wounded. Iran has criticized upcoming US economic sanctions as an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty, while the US military has helped facilitate the transit of millions of barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
key_points: US President Donald Trump stated that Iran is not ready to make the right deal despite wanting an agreement.
The Pentagon reported 18 US service members killed and 756 wounded in the war against Iran.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei condemned imminent US economic sanctions as lacking foundation in international law.
Iran agreed to allow certain Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz to protect Iraq's economic interests.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright stated that the US military helped transit over 15 million barrels of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz.

title: As Russian missiles rain down on Kyiv, casualties mount and the mood darkens
author: Dan Sabbagh; Julia Kochetova
content:
Viktor, 23, Sofiia, 18, and their dog, Teddy, were bedding down for the night on Thursday at the Dorohozhychi metro station three stops from Kyiv’s city centre. The couple have sheltered here “every night for the past three weeks”, Viktor said, as the missile threat to the city worsened; the dog, only three months old, has been with them a fortnight. Teddy lies quietly, knowing no different a life.
![People sleeping inside Dorohozhychi subway station.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ace653bff5dacc79b4205af3fbeb689c90f6165f/0_0_3694_2467/master/3694.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  People sleeping at Dorohozhychi metro station for safety.
The atmosphere in the Ukrainian capital has shifted in the past couple of months as the war has returned more sharply to the home front. Russian high-speed ballistic missiles are routinely targeting the city and Ukraine’s military have run out of the interceptors from the only weapon system that can stop them, US-made Patriots. The anxiety that hangs over the wartime city has intensified.
![Two people clear debris from around a damaged car](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e9c48523c40b9dbda9aead11c03f774e48f60c6a/0_0_4240_2832/master/4240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
![People make their way past wreckage after a Russian attack on Solomyanskiy district](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2468f20872e6f52c43e6dd6195e0740c879941c7/0_0_4240_2832/master/4240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
![Emergency workers and civilians after a Russian attack on Solomyanskiy district](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4ebdd5eabf8673cafe388b36455264b089f83e88/600_391_3385_2431/master/3385.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
![A woman sits among other people near the site of the attack on Solomyanskiy district](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/85dc8418b92976a45af35f78b34b09ab4aa40720/24_0_4902_3549/master/4902.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  (Clockwise from top left): Vitalii clears debris from around his damaged car with the help of a neighbour; the aftermath of a Russian night attack on Solomyanskiy district; a woman rests near the site of the attack.
“Before, if you heard an air-raid warning you still had time to pack your stuff and get to the shelter. Now you have a warning and then in 30 seconds you have explosions, so you have no time,” Sofiia said. A night earlier, a wave of missiles targeted the city within minutes of the first warning, at 11.51pm. Sixteen people were reported killed after the missiles struck locations including residential blocks in the suburbs. Warnings of drone attacks followed for several more hours, fraying nerves after the opening hits.
City dwellers had been fearing a big attack on Wednesday night. It had been a few days since the last one – and there were also reports that Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers were flying to the war zone. They launch cruise missiles, but their presence in the air heralds a wider missile and drone attack. The lower hall at Dorohozhychi metro was packed by 10pm that night, Viktor said, with tents or people lying on ground sheets, almost no space left for the couple as they arrived.
Earlier on Thursday, in the morning, the grim aftermath of the missile strikes on residential areaswas clearly visible. Two missiles struck the Solomianskyi district west of the centre, one shearing off the top floor of a 10-storey apartment block, killing two people, the second crashing into a disused building in the centre of a car park, reducing it to a scatter of rubble, while local people tried to see if there was any hope for their cars – the ones that were not completely burnt out.
The rear end of Vitalii’s car was smashed in by the blast, and it appears to be a write-off. The 42-year-old said he works for an insurance company, yet admitted he had not insured his own vehicle. After a while, however, the car started, remarkably, its engine having faced away from the blast. At first the impact of the overnight attack may be financial, but Vitalii said its real effect will be psychological. “We are alive, our arms and legs whole. We will go on. But now it will be more scary.”
![Vitalii, in Kyiv, is checking his damaged car](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6ddfd2ca5fba1981aba596520c1f3223afc39c4b/700_0_3540_2832/master/3540.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
![A woman sits out in the open in the aftermath of the airstrike](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f77e5d38686d8505ffd2421dac4d0a514663ba78/650_185_4188_3375/master/4188.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  Vitalii, a Kyiv resident, checks his damaged car; a woman rests and checks her phone the day after the Russian attack.
Kyiv’s mayor, the former champion heavyweight Vitali Klitschko, arrived on the scene. “These attacks on the city have one aim – to drive people into depression,” he said. He is pressed about how many new bomb shelters the city has built, which might avoid people having to sleep in metro stations that reopen at 6am. He could offer no figure to one questioner.
![Vitali Klitschko, Kyiv’s city mayor, talks to the media at the site of a direct hit](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c2d1c9c0d884a919e8c875de4a44c8c4705bd0bd/320_0_3517_2487/master/3517.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  Vitali Klitschko, Kyiv’s city mayor, talks to the media at the site of a direct hit.
Ukraine’s military no longer announces how many ballistics come in because it cannot stop them, though hits can easily heard from bedrooms right across the capital. In July, the last full month for which figures are available, 437 civilians were killed across Ukraine and 2,610 injured according to UN figures – the highest number recorded killed since May 2022.
Though it is August and the daily temperatures are frequently in the 30s, much of the talk is about the winter to come, when people expect to lose central heating and electricity as so many homes did last year when apartment temperatures in the worst-affected districts dropped to 4-5C. Kyiv’s infrastructure appears defenceless and those who can have long bought generators, batteries, electric radiators and anything else for emergency heating, but worries linger.
![A survivor holds a backpack with her cat near the place of the night attack in Solomyanskiy district](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/fb43c86d684e6c66c122ec2f52b07c9e121b0e19/765_423_2992_2174/master/2992.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  A survivor of the night’s attacks holds a backpack containing her cat in Solomyanskiy district.
“We are prepared to cope without electricity and without central heating – we did our homework, prepared the apartment and lasted last dreadful winter,” said Maria Hlazunova, who lives in the centre of the city. “But water … I’m afraid of lacking the opportunity to wash hands and food properly. Not to mention the toilet,” which she acknowledges is a particular source of anxiety. Residents know the city has only one wastewater treatment site, at Bortnychi. It has not yet been hit.
Ukraine has defended itself by stepping up its attacks on Russia, long-range targeting first of the country’s oil refineries, leading to queues at petrol stations, and more recently by targeting warehouses, e-commerce sites that Kyiv says are also used by the military for logistics. It has been effective, though Russia has responded in kind – bombing and destroying warehouses just outside Kyiv, the medium-term economic consequences from the destruction uncertain.
![A huge warehouse in Brovary, Kyiv region, after it was damaged by an airstrike](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a2a9588cb0a196554d1e7ccc06338a9957dc2612/223_0_4017_2832/master/4017.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
![A firefighter sprays water on the warehouse after the Russian attack in Kyiv region](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/dbc3180c3d4d2c407afed4e633cd9a40f25235f2/0_0_5000_3505/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  The damaged Rozetka warehouse in Brovary, Kyiv region; a firefighter works at the warehouse after a Russian attack.
Early on Thursday, a food distribution warehouse near Ukraine’s unused Boryspil commercial airport was completely destroyed by a missile attack. The fire spread because a succession of drone warnings – Shaheds were flying above – meant that emergency workers could not safely attend at first. When the Guardian visited in the afternoon, parts of the burnt-out site were still smouldering, and there were a handful of employees who recognised their jobs had disappeared in the wreckage.
Viktoriia Ruban, the spokesperson for Ukraine’s state emergency services in Kyiv region, the area just outside the city, described a change in Russian military tactics. “Previously, the Russians would strike the Kyiv region at night. Now it’s three or four hours, then a strike; another three or four hours, then another strike. Whether it’s morning or daytime – it makes no difference now,” she said, and the observation applies also to the capital city where daytime alerts have become more common.
Iryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, Ukraine’s most successful e-commerce distributor, showed a few journalists around the ruins of what was her company’s largest distribution hub near Brovary, north-east of Kyiv. It was a modern automated facility, built for $70m, capable of sending 100,000 parcels a day, and employing 1,000. But it was totally destroyed by three missiles on the night of August 4-5, the inferno so great that in places only bent-over cranes can be made out.
![Iryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, inside the burnt-out distribution hub of her company in Brovary, Kyiv region](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a2efa3758785abd16edc6cbbbede0c5ee73ca3c9/0_0_5000_3750/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
- 
  Iryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, inside her company’s burnt-out distribution hub in Brovary, Kyiv region.
It was a clearly difficult visit for the businesswoman, amid worries that more of the company’s warehouses could be struck, affecting Rozetka and the 50,000 vendors who rely on its service. But the wider military reality is fragile.
“How can a country defend itself against ballistic threats if we have nothing with which to shoot them down?” she asked. “It’s very hard for me; I’m a mother of four and I’ve sacrificed time with them to build this place. It’s my life’s work.” Breaking into English, she added: “This is not easy.”
summary: Intense Russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv have left residents facing mounting casualties, widespread psychological distress, and a lack of defense systems like US-made Patriots to intercept fast ballistic threats. The strikes have destroyed residential buildings, car parks, and major economic infrastructure, including a massive e-commerce distribution hub near Brovary. As the autumn and winter approach, city dwellers are increasingly anxious about potential infrastructure failures and the ongoing danger of unannounced daytime and nighttime strikes.
key_points: Russian high-speed ballistic missiles are routinely targeting Kyiv, and Ukrainian forces have run out of US-made Patriot interceptors to stop them.
Recent overnight and daytime strikes have damaged residential blocks, killed civilians, and destroyed key commercial infrastructure such as a $70m Rozetka distribution hub.
Kyiv residents are increasingly taking shelter in metro stations nightly as air-raid warnings leave virtually no time to react before explosions occur.
Concerns are growing among locals regarding the upcoming winter and potential losses of central heating, electricity, and water supplies.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko noted that the attacks aim to drive people into depression, while residents and business owners grapple with deep psychological and financial impacts.

title: Father leaves 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji to continue hike, reports say
author: Dan Sales
content:
![Mount Fuji is pictured from the skies with a ring of white cloud bordering the frame of the image](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/b92b/live/3baa1370-9dfb-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
The boy was found alone on Japan's highest mountain
- Published
A father has been reprimanded by police after leaving his son on Japan's highest mountain for several hours with just a soft drink and snack, local media report.
The seven-year-old was spotted sitting on a bench on Mount Fuji in foggy and rainy conditions, at a point situated at over 2,000m (6,500ft).
His father, 48, reportedly told him to "wait here" after the boy complained he was tired - and continued the climb with his elder son.
Staff at a mountain hut found the child near the sixth station of a hiking route towards the summit and alerted police. His father was tracked down at the route's eighth station - said to be a three-hour hike away.
According to reports, the boy was found on his own at 07:30 local time on Thursday (22:30 GMT).
Officers castigated his father when he returned from the higher station and reunited with his son.
"Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable," one told him, according to Japan Today. He is said to have apologised for the "rash" decision.
The family was reported to have been on the Fujinomiya route, which starts from the fifth station on the mountain, a spot which is accessible by public transport.
From there it takes around five hours to reach the peak and a further three hours to get down, climbing guides suggest.
Mount Fuji, which stands at a height of 3,776m (12,389ft), has been the site of a number of climbing mishaps in recent years.
In July, a 99-year-old woman had to be rescued attempting the route after falling and hurting her hip and back.
And last year, a 27-year-old university student who went outside of official climbing season had to be rescued twice in four days - after he went back to look for his lost mobile phone.
Mount Fuji, an active volcano located south-west of Tokyo, was granted World Heritage status in 2013.
It is also one of three traditional "Holy Mountains" together with Mount Tate and Mount Haku.
Around 200,000 people climb it each year, but there are daily caps on some routes to avoid overcrowding.
summary: A father in Japan was reprimanded by police after leaving his seven-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji for several hours. The boy, who was given only a soft drink and a snack, was found sitting on a bench in rainy and foggy conditions over 2,000 meters up the mountain. His father had continued climbing with his older son after the younger child complained of being tired.
key_points: A 48-year-old father left his seven-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji after the boy said he was tired.
The child was found by mountain hut staff at an elevation of over 2,000 meters in rainy and foggy weather.
The father was located by police at the eighth station of the hiking route, a three-hour hike away from where the boy was left.
Officers castigated the father for his rash decision, and he subsequently apologized.

title: TikTok agrees to $400m settlement to resolve US children’s privacy litigation
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
TikTok and its Chinese former parent company ByteDance on Friday agreed to a $400m settlement to resolve the US Department of Justice’s allegations that the short-form video app violated children’s online privacy.
The justice department sued TikTok and ByteDance in 2024 for allegedly failing to protect children’s privacy and illegally collecting their information. The defendants were accused of violating a law requiring online services aimed at children to obtain parental consent to collect personal information from users under age 13.
Associate attorney general Stanley Woodward said the justice department’s priority “is ensuring that children are protected online and that companies entrusted with their personal information meet their legal obligations”.
TikTok did not immediately comment.
Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300m immediately and an additional $100m upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in 2019 against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly. As part of the consent agreement, the FTC said that TikTok, then known as Musical.ly, knew that young children used the app and had failed to get parental consent to collect their names, email addresses and other personal information. It paid a fine of $5.7m.
In January, ByteDance agreed to establish a majority American-owned joint venture to secure US data and avoid a ban on the app used by more than 200 million Americans. The government noted that since the complaint was filed, TikTok has undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions and privacy practices.
DoJ said the settlement “ensures that American families continue to benefit from stronger protections without the delay and uncertainty of protracted litigation”. The TikTok US joint venture said in a court filing it requires all users to enter their date of birth to use the site.
after newsletter promotion
TikTok said it has developed sophisticated age-moderation systems that identify children under 13 who misrepresented their age. That court filing said that TikTok has hundreds of personnel trained in underage moderation and, as a result, deletes tens of thousands underage accounts.
summary: TikTok and its former parent company ByteDance have agreed to a $400 million settlement to resolve US Department of Justice allegations that they violated children's online privacy. The lawsuit accused the companies of failing to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from users under 13. Under the agreement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million if a prior 2019 FTC consent decree is vacated.
key_points: TikTok and ByteDance agreed to a $400 million settlement with the US Department of Justice.
The lawsuit alleged the app violated laws by collecting personal data from children under 13 without parental consent.
TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and $100 million upon the entry of an order vacating a 2019 FTC consent decree.
TikTok has since implemented age-moderation systems, requires birth dates, and deletes tens of thousands of underage accounts.

title: Canada says it will match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' as trade talks break down
author: Nadine Yousif; Toby Mann
content:
![Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney attends the announcement of a Quebec-Newfoundland hydro agreement](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/ef5d/live/88423690-9ddd-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Prime Minister Mark Carney said progress in the talks was not enough to meet Canada's objectives
- Published
A fresh wave of US tariffs on a wide array of Canadian goods came into effect on Saturday after a last-minute breakdown in trade talks.
Announcing the suspension of negotiations shortly before the Friday night deadline, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he would impose reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar".
Carney said "last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal".
Trade negotiators had been engaged in intense talks since July, after President Donald Trump threatened to impose a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian imports by 19 August.
Trump had temporarily paused those tariffs earlier in the week, saying the two sides were close to signing a trade deal that was "very good" for both countries.
But minutes before the deadline for a deal, Carney said that while "important progress" had been made in the talks it was "not enough to meet our objectives for Canadians".
"As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed negotiators to return to Ottawa," he said.
"Last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."
After Carney's announcement US trade representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement: "Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.
"Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days."
The breakdown in talks marks a significant shift in tone from earlier in the week, when both US and Canadian officials sounded optimistic that a trade deal beneficial for both countries was within reach.
Negotiators were reportedly discussing a deal that would reduce US tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminium from 50% to 25%, and on Canadian autos from 25% to 15%.
In exchange, Carney had asked Canadian provinces to restore US alcohol to store shelves.
Tensions between the two major trading partners have been simmering since Trump returned to office in January last year and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs, upending decades of free trade between Canada and the US.
Now that talks have broken down, Canada will be hit with new 50% US tariffs imposed by Trump using a Depression-era law called the Tariff Act of 1930.
They will be applied on a range of goods, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.
They are in addition to existing tariffs the US had already imposed on Canadian steel and aluminium, autos and lumber.
Doug Ford, the traditionally outspoken premier of Canada's largest province Ontario, said "the prime minister has my full support for a strong response - tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," following Carney's announcement.
Canada has been engaged in on-again, off-again trade negotiations with the US for over a year in pursuit of a deal that would see the US drop or reduce tariffs on these key sectors.
The US, meanwhile, has been asking for a number of concessions from Canada, including removing its remaining retaliatory tariffs on American autos and adjusting its dairy quotas to allow greater access for US cheese producers.
It has also asked that the ban on US alcohol sales, imposed last year by most Canadian provinces in retaliation to Trump's tariffs, be removed.
Businesses and stakeholders on both sides of the border had pushed for a deal to be reached, arguing that the new US tariffs on Canada will be harmful to both countries.
The US Chamber of Commerce said earlier in the week in a statement that "higher tariffs would damage both economies, drive up costs for US families, further disrupt critical supply chains, and risk the 13 million American jobs that depend on trade under the US-Mexico-Canada Trade Agreement".
A recent poll by Canadian firm Abacus Data suggested that around 36% of Canadians would support retaliating to US tariffs, while another 30% would want the Carney government to continue negotiating.
Retaliation risks upsetting the Trump administration, with trade representative Jamieson Greer saying the US is "not going to tolerate" counter-tariffs.
"We'll take action," he told reporters last week.
summary: Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed after last-minute changes to proposed terms by the US, leading to the implementation of a fresh wave of US tariffs on Canadian goods. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended negotiations and announced that Canada will impose reciprocal tariffs on US goods dollar for dollar. The breakdown ends a period of optimism and renews trade tensions that have simmered since President Donald Trump returned to office.
key_points: A fresh wave of US tariffs on Canadian goods came into effect after trade talks broke down just before the deadline.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the suspension of negotiations and promised dollar-for-dollar reciprocal tariffs on US goods.
Carney stated that last-minute US terms were unfair, uneconomic, and unreliable.
The US trade representative claimed Canada declined to finalize the deal due to new demands and retracted commitments.
The new 50% US tariffs apply to goods including wine, dairy, cement, clothing, and hockey equipment.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy vows response to Russia’s deadly shopping centre attack
author: Agencies; Guardian staff reporter
content:
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit back at Russia after its deadly attack on a shopping centre in central Ukraine. At least 16 people were killed and more than 130 wounded, authorities said, when drones on hit the mall in Kryvyi Rih in what the Ukrainian president called a “cynical and despicable” attack on Friday. In an evening video post on social media, Zelenskyy said of the strikes in his home town: “An absolute Russian atrocity. They’re just monsters. We will definitely respond.” He added: “It is important that we have everything to protect life. It is important that the world does not remain silent about all this. There must be an end to this Russian war – and we need the world to help us make that happen.” The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, condemned the attack as “terror by design” and threatened “the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war”. Four more people, including three minors, were killed in another strike in the southern Mykolaiv region on Friday, said the interior minister, Ivan Vygivsky.
- 
  Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least two people early on Saturday, local authorities said. The Kyiv city military administration reported a fire in a warehouse in the capital’s Darnytskyi district after issuing an alert for a ballistic missile. One person died and several were injured, it said, citing preliminary information. In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, a Russian drone killed a man and wounded four people, according to the regional military administration’s chief, Ivan Fedorov.
- 
  Countries allied with Ukraine are to meet on Monday to reaffirm support for Kyiv in the war, at talks held on Ukraine’s independence day. The meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing will be co-chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. About 10 leaders including the European Council chief, António Costa, will be in Kyiv for the meeting, according to an EU official. Zelenskyy urged a strong response from Ukraine’s allies after Russia’s shopping centre attack, saying: “The world must respond to them accordingly – with real pressure on the aggressor. For peace to be possible, Russia must face real accountability.”
- 
  Germany is seeking to extradite a suspect from Romania over the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence, reports Deborah Cole. Two weeks after German authorities found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”. “This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level,” Alexander Dobrindt told reporters.
- 
  Ukraine has sanctioned Russian hit children’s cartoon Masha and the Bear and its producers in a step towards banning the series, the Ukrainian culture minister said on Friday, slamming it as a Russian “propaganda” tool. The cartoon about a little girl and a retired circus bear has been viewed tens of billions of times on YouTube alone and broadcast in about 100 countries but has faced criticism in Ukraine and among its allies, including the UK and Estonia, as painting Russia in a positive light. The Kremlin has laughed off the allegations.
![Firefighters work at the site of a shopping centre hit by a Russian drones attack in Kryvyi Rih, central Ukraine, killing at least 16 people.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b6d6cb49af17646a83f3a51ed2ee73cd48cd31a7/48_0_1065_852/master/1065.jpg?width=465&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Ukrainian president calls strikes on home town Kryvyi Rih an ‘absolute Russian atrocity’ and says world must ‘not remain silent’. What we know on day 1,641
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy vowed a strong response after a deadly Russian drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih killed at least 16 people and wounded over 130. Additional Russian strikes across Ukraine resulted in more casualties, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas condemned the mall attack and threatened new sanctions. Meanwhile, international allies are scheduled to meet in Kyiv to reaffirm support, and Germany is investigating a weapons cache linked to potential threats against national security.
key_points: A Russian drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih killed at least 16 people and wounded over 130.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas condemned the attack as "terror by design" and warned of significant new sanctions.
Separate Russian strikes in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia killed at least two more people early on Saturday.
Leaders from allied nations are set to meet in Kyiv on Monday to discuss continued support for Ukraine.
Ukraine sanctioned the popular Russian cartoon Masha and the Bear, labeling it a propaganda tool.

title: Attack on Ukraine shopping centre that killed 16 is ‘terror by design’, says EU foreign policy chief
author: Agence France-Presse; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Russian drones have slammed into a busy shopping centre in central Ukraine, killing 16 people in an attack that Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned as “cynical and despicable”.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, condemned Friday’s attack on Kryvyi Rih – the president’s home town – as “terror by design” and said she was “putting forward the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war” when ministers meet in Ireland next month.
“Russia’s attack against a shopping centre in [Kryvyi Rih] shows the absolute and utter depravity of Moscow’s war,” Kallas said on X, claiming that Moscow “wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable”.
The strike comes as Russia has intensified its bombardments of Ukrainian cities in recent months. Separately, four more people, including three children, were killed in another strike in the southern Mykolaiv region, the interior minister, Ivan Vygivsky, said on Telegram.
Videos on social media of the Kryvyi Rih attack showed rescuers rushing to help the wounded on the street outside, as smoke poured out of the building.
A second drone smashed into the roof of the building about half an hour after the first – a repeat strike that Zelenskyy said in a post on X was “targeting the emergency responders”.
Ukrainian emergency services initially said the attack had killed 15 people and wounded 130 others, 23 of them children.
The head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration, Oleksandr Ganzha, later said on Telegram the death toll had risen to 16.
In his X post, Zelenskyy condemned “an absolutely cynical and despicable strike ... carried out by the Russians against an ordinary shopping centre”.
![The shopping centre in the aftermath of the Russian attack](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5b9d2961ce6d33b488967b58b70ad771b5725563/0_0_1346_1077/master/1346.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Kryvyi Rih, an industrial city about 60km (37 miles) from the front line, has come under repeated Russian attacks throughout the war.
Ukraine’s allies are to meet on Monday to reaffirm their support for Kyiv in talks held on the country’s independence day. The meeting of the so-called “coalition of the willing” will be co-chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz.
About 10 leaders including the European Council chief, António Costa, will be in Kyiv for the coalition meeting, according to an EU official.
Zelenskyy urged a strong response from Ukraine’s allies.
“The world must respond to them accordingly – with real pressure on the aggressor. For peace to be possible, Russia must face real accountability,” he said.
Zelenskyy held a call with the UN chief, António Guterres, on Friday, updating him on Russian strikes and the civilian casualties they had caused, the Ukrainian leader said on X.
Kyiv has repeatedly appealed to its allies for additional support as Russia steps up its strikes, with Ukrainian forces struggling in particular to intercept salvos of ballistic missiles.
summary: Russian drone strikes on a busy shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine, killed 16 people and injured numerous others, with a second drone targeting emergency responders. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas labeled it 'terror by design' and proposed sweeping new sanctions against Russia. The incident coincides with intensified Russian bombardments across Ukrainian cities and ongoing appeals from Kyiv for increased international support and accountability.
key_points: Russian drones hit a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih, killing 16 people and injuring many, including children.
A second drone struck the building roughly 30 minutes later, specifically targeting emergency responders.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas condemned the attack as 'terror by design' and announced plans for major new Russia sanctions.
A separate strike in the Mykolaiv region killed four people, including three children.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for a strong international response and real accountability for Russia.

title: Boy, 7, left alone on Mount Fuji by his own dad
author: Emily Bashforth
content:
![This photo taken on January 30, 2024 shows an aerial view of Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 meters (12,389 feet), from the window of a passenger jet. An online booking system for Mount Fuji's most popular trail was announced on May 13, 2024 by Japanese authorities trying to fight overtourism on the active volcano. (Photo by Richard A. Brooks / AFP) (Photo by RICHARD A. BROOKS/AFP via Getty Images)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_203864832-8d23.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘Wait here,’ is what a dad told his seven-year-old son before leaving him alone on Mount Fuji and continuing his hike.
The boy had been making his way to the summit with his father and older brother on Thursday morning via the Fujinomiya Trail.
He complained of feeling tired at the sixth station, which is at an altitude of approximately 2,490 metres and at least five hours from the summit, but his dad decided not to pause to rest or turn back.
Instead, he instructed him to stay put while he carried on the ascent with his other son, a first-year middle school student.
Hours later, the first-grader from Nagoya, Japan, was found by a mountain hut worker.
He was sitting on a bench at around 7.40am, with hiking time estimates suggesting his father had left him at roughly 4.30am.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
![Japan's highest mountain, Mount Fuji, 3,776 metres (12,388 feet), seen from a commercial flight in Japan, July 29, 2026. REUTERS/Issei Kato](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_306794057-8171.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
As fog began to gather and rain fell, it sparked concerns, as weather conditions on the mountain can change quickly, so the worker brought the boy inside for shelter and called the police.
Authorities were thankfully able to reach the father, who had made it to the eighth station, where police urged him to abandon his climb and collect his son.
Upon being reunited, the boy’s father was scolded by police: ‘Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable.’
- 
	![16060309 Alex McCarthy died in the collision in Co Kildare in the early hours of Sunday morningAlex McCarthyFor Dan Sanderson](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308733309-7680.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- Boy, 15, killed in wrong-way motorway crash is carried in gold coffin at his funeral
- Row of supercars petrol bombed during wedding in Birmingham
- Woman, 38, pretended to be 11 years old to trick couple into adopting her
The man expressed remorse, saying: ‘I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it.’
Fortunately, the boy was unharmed.
Police also issued reminders to other hiking groups, telling them to stay together and set their pace based on the person with the least stamina or the least physically capable.
Mount Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan and its most popular hiking period is July to August. Around 200,000-300,000 people climb the mountain each summer.
Get in touch with our news team by emailing us at webnews@metro.co.uk.
For more stories like this, check our news page.
summary: A father in Japan left his seven-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji after the boy became tired and complained during their hike. The boy was found hours later by a mountain hut worker who sheltered him from worsening weather and contacted the police. Authorities located the father at a higher station, ordered him to abandon the climb, and scolded him for the unacceptable behavior.
key_points: A father left his seven-year-old son alone at the sixth station of Mount Fuji after the boy grew tired.
The father continued the climb with his older son instead of turning back or resting.
A mountain hut worker found the boy, brought him inside due to worsening weather, and called the police.
Police contacted the father at the eighth station, ordered him to abort the climb, and scolded him for leaving the child.
The boy was unharmed, and the father later expressed deep regret for his rash decision.

title: 'We have more work to do', says Canada negotiator as US trade deadline looms
author: Nadine Yousif
content:
![Dominic LeBlanc, in a suit and tie, speaks to reporters as he stands outside the  doors to the US trade representative's office](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/064f/live/86495a50-9dbd-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington for two weeks trying to hammer out a deal
- Published
Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said negotiators "have more work to do" as he left a meeting with US counterparts ahead of a midnight deadline to finalise a tentative trade deal with the Trump administration.
"We're going to continue working up until the last minute," he told reporters in Washington on Friday evening. "Our job is not finished."
Negotiators have until Friday night to hammer out the details of the deal or risk a fresh wave of additional US tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods.
LeBlanc spent some eight hours in meetings with US trade representative Jamieson Greer and other negotiators - one of the longest sessions so far as talks go down to the wire.
Hours before the deadline, President Donald Trump did not say whether a definitive deal had been agreed, but that it was "moving along".
"We should be able to have a deal with Canada. We're also starting on a new deal with Mexico. A much better deal for the United States. I only make good deals," he told reporters on Friday.
The full framework of the deal has yet to be made public, but details leaked to several media outlets suggest the US will agree to reduce tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminium from 50% to 25%, and tariffs on Canadian automobiles from 25% to 15%.
In addition to restoring the sale of American alcohol, Canada is said to be considering allowing American dairy producers greater access to its market and removing its retaliatory tariffs on the US.
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said that any agreement that includes "one-sided" tariffs on Canadian industry is "a bad deal".
"I am concerned with the de-industrialisation of our economy if our key industries pay one-sided tariffs," Poilievre told reporters on Friday.
One of Canada's provincial leaders has criticised a prospective trade deal with the US and pushed his country to hold out for favourable terms, showing Prime Minister Mark Carney faces a tough battle in getting buy-in on the agreement hours away from a US-set deadline.
Still, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said Canada "should fight" and not rush to make concessions.
Carney needs Kinew and other premiers to restore sales of US alcohol on liquor store shelves, so that the US will reportedly agree to reduce some of its tariffs on Canadian metals and autos.
![An image showing Wab Kinew speaking in front of several microphones at a press conference with a few of Canada's other premiers behind him. He has black hair that is tied up in a bun, and is wearing a dark charcoal grey suit and tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/768e/live/ffd477b0-9d68-11f1-a07c-85afe5c51b6f.jpg)
Manitoba premier Wab Kinew publicly criticised the trade deal being discussed by the US and Canada, and called Donald Trump a "bad person"
Quebec Premier Christine FrÃ©chette, whose province is home to a large dairy industry, said on Thursday that she was analysing what the deal will mean for Quebec farmers before deciding on whether to restore US alcohol sales.
Doug Ford, the traditionally outspoken premier of Canada's largest province Ontario, has yet to comment publicly on the deal.
Meanwhile, other premiers, namely of Nova Scotia and the Yukon territory, said they were prepared to restore US alcohol sales.
The mayor of an Ontario city that is home to the country's second-largest steel producer told the CBC that a deal that includes 25% tariffs on the sector "wouldn't be something to celebrate".
"I am worried with the news that's coming out that we are not seeing a deal that will benefit our community at the very least," Mayor Matthew Shoemaker said.
But Carney has also faced pressure from businesses and stakeholders to reach a deal that would avert an additional 50% tariff that Trump has threatened on a range of Canadian goods, from hockey equipment to wine to cement.
Canada could lose 90,000 jobs if the new tariffs were implemented, according to estimates in an analysis published on Thursday, external by Trevor Tombe, a Calgary-based economist.
The mixed reaction so far is a glimpse of the task ahead for Prime Minister Carney after he campaigned on a tough "elbows-up" approach to dealing with Trump.
Polls suggest a majority of Canadians would be unhappy if the Carney government made significant concessions to the US, with 56% surveyed by polling firm Leger, external saying they wanted Canada to take a hardline approach.
In a leaked audio recording reported by the Canadian Press, US Vice-President JD Vance told attendees at a private fundraiser on Wednesday that Carney has tried to "out-tough Donald Trump" in trade talks.
"It's hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory for Canada when fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues," Vance reportedly told the room.
summary: Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc stated that negotiators have more work to do as they approach a midnight deadline to finalize a tentative trade deal with the Trump administration. The prospective agreement could see the US reduce tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, and automobiles, while Canada considers granting greater dairy market access and removing retaliatory tariffs. However, Prime Minister Mark Carney faces internal challenges as several provincial premiers and local leaders express criticism and concern over potential concessions and one-sided tariffs.
key_points: Canadian trade minister Dominic LeBlanc and US counterparts engaged in extended meetings in Washington ahead of a midnight trade deal deadline.
Leaked details suggest the US may reduce tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum to 25% and autos to 15%, while Canada considers removing retaliatory tariffs and offering dairy market access.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and other critics voiced concerns over rushing into a deal and making one-sided concessions to the US.
Prime Minister Carney faces pressure from businesses to avoid a threatened fresh wave of US tariffs that could risk thousands of Canadian jobs.

title: US supreme court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
author: Marina Dunbar
content:
The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue construction of his controversial White House ballroom for now, temporarily pausing a lower court order that would halt much of the project.
Supreme court chief justice John Roberts signed a temporary order on Friday, permitting work to continue on the planned White House addition – a top priority of the president – while the court considers an emergency appeal from Trump’s administration.
Democrats accused the supreme court, which is controlled by a conservative super-majority, of “rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption”. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said: “As costs skyrocket, the administration is wasting money on an endless and illegal war, corporate giveaways and Trump’s pet projects.”
The president swiftly welcomed the order, which puts the Friday deadline from the appeals court on pause. That court had ordered construction to stop while a legal challenge proceeded, after concluding earlier this month that the ballroom project probably requires congressional approval before work can continue.
The Trump administration then turned to the supreme court, arguing that construction of the structure was critical to national security and the safety of the US president.
On Tuesday, the National Trust for Historic Preservation had urged the supreme court to suspend the ballroom project following an earlier lawsuit seeking to block construction.
The massive 90,000sq-ft (8,400 sq meters) ballroom project part of the president’s sprawling plans to reshape the nation’s capital, has already involved the demolition of the White House East Wing. Construction also includes an underground military facility that the administration says is needed to protect the president.
The underground military bunker would be a five-story complex that will include shelters, a hospital and other features designed to protect the president and senior officials during an emergency.
The total cost of the project is expected to exceed $400m.
“It is something that Presidents have wanted for 150 years, and that the Military has been seeking for the last 100 years,” Trump claimed in a social media post on Friday. “Their wish will soon be fulfilled! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule.”
Administration officials say the ballroom itself will be reinforced with missile-resistant columns and a drone-proof roof, allowing the structure to serve as a shield for both the underground military complex and the wider White House.
Construction on the ballroom has been under way for 10 months with the administration saying the project is now approximately 65% complete.
The administration has argued that authority over White House renovations is held by the president, not Congress or the courts. The justice department also argued that leaving the site in its current condition, effectively an open construction zone, makes protecting the White House more difficult.
summary: The US Supreme Court has temporarily allowed Donald Trump to continue construction on a controversial White House ballroom project while considering an emergency administration appeal. Chief Justice John Roberts signed the order pausing a lower court ruling that would have halted the project over a lack of congressional approval. The administration defends the 90,000 sq ft project, which includes a five-story underground military complex, as vital for national security and presidential protection.
key_points: Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts signed a temporary order allowing White House ballroom construction to continue.
The administration argued the project is critical for national security and presidential safety.
The 90,000 sq ft project includes a five-story underground military complex and is expected to cost over $400m.
Democrats strongly criticized the Supreme Court's decision, accusing the administration of wasting money on pet projects.
Construction has been underway for 10 months and is currently estimated to be about 65% complete.

title: ‘Shameful’: UK, Australia and Canada criticise Israel over Gaza aid convoy killings decision
author: Jason Burke
content:
Britain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”. The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation.
WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage.
“This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,” the countries’ joint statement said.
It continued: “In Gaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.”
On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision.
The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties.
In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.
WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air.
“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.
The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.
One of the officers who was dismissed had reportedly signed an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid. Israel imposed strict restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance during the conflict in Gaza, where experts declared a famine in August 2025.
The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025.
Hind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.
The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.
The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions.
summary: The UK, Australia, and Canada have issued a joint statement condemning the Israeli military's decision not to launch a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers. The allied nations and victim families criticized the internal military process as lacking accountability, while the IDF defended its conclusion that the actions did not constitute criminal misconduct. Meanwhile, Poland expressed disappointment and called for cooperation with its own investigation into the death of a Polish volunteer.
key_points: The UK, Australia, and Canada labeled the Israeli military's decision not to criminally investigate the WCK convoy strikes as shameful.
Seven humanitarian workers from the World Central Kitchen were killed in the April 2024 airstrikes in Gaza.
The IDF stated it mistook individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas operatives and concluded commanders showed no criminal misconduct.
WCK and families of the victims criticized the decision as lacking accountability and being inconsistent with the truth.
Poland expressed disappointment over the decision and demanded cooperation with Polish investigations.

title: Aliens at 40: from wearable cameras to exoskeletons, here are the technologies the film predicted
author: Steve Benford
content:
Director James Cameron’s acclaimed sci-fi movie Aliens turns 40 in August. It’s a sequel to Ridley Scott’s claustrophobic breakout hit Alien, made in 1979. Where the original featured one terrifying creature, Cameron’s movie features hundreds – and pits them against a squad of space marines.
A host of intriguing technologies make an appearance, including interstellar travel, hypersleep (where humans are preserved in stasis for long space journeys) and terraforming (making other worlds liveable for humans).
Some of the technologies in the film have already come to pass – or look likely to soon. But others were missed and some remain firmly in the realms of science fiction.
In Aliens, the marines travel to a distant moon to investigate the disappearance of over 100 human settlers. Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver), the main protagonist of the first film, goes along to advise.
On arrival, they run into a six-year-old girl, called Newt, who managed to escape the grisly fate of the other colonists. When the marines encounter the alien hive, chaos and carnage ensue.
The technology featured in Aliens appears to be there to support the wonderful storytelling, rather than predict the path of innovation, as a futurologist might.
But let’s take a look at it. The film is set in 2179, 153 years into our future. Journeying 153 years into the past would land us in 1893, when common technologies were horse drawn and steam streetcars and gas lighting. Typewriters with Qwerty keyboards went on sale the following year.
Industrial aesthetic
We’ve moved on considerably, but the future world of Aliens feels less distant in many respects. Company executives use clunky business cards to trigger low-resolution video calls and wave computer printouts during meeting room showdowns.
For modern audiences, however, the lack of personal electronic devices may be jarring. One can only assume that they must have fallen out of favour by 2179.
The gritty, industrial visual style established in the first film was taken further here. Aliens introduces a variety of military vehicles that contain futuristic elements while drawing on real hardware used in the Vietnam war. The movie’s look influenced later films, but it has also been described as “everyday” and “ugly”.
An exception is the tracking technology: the motion detectors, wearable cameras and biosensors embedded into wristbands. These feel broadly “current”. But if we extrapolate from the present day, one might expect engineers in 2179 to make greater use of surveillance cameras and computer vision (a sub-field of AI where machines are trained to “understand” images and video).
A network of “smart cameras” throughout the moon colony could have tracked both the aliens and humans. Similar networks today monitor crowds and individuals – and watch for suspicious behaviour – on city streets and public transport.
Sentry guns and exoskeletons
The robots of Aliens are striking. Some are not so far removed from hardware used today, but with notable differences. In two separate scenes, Ripley straps into a massive mechanical suit known as a “loader”.
They are mainly used to move cargo, but, conveniently, can be appropriated for fighting xenomorphs. The loaders are a type of exoskeleton, real life wearable tech that may enhance human strength or movement.
Exoskeletons aren’t generally used for this kind of task yet. Large autonomous or teleoperated factory robots are the go-to technology for lifting heavy hardware. This is safer than having humans operate in such hazardous environments.
Current exoskeletons are smaller in scale than the loaders. They are helping people walk again after traumatic injury and commercial versions are available to support those with mobility issues to hill walk.
The war in Ukraine, meanwhile, has familiarised us with autonomous combat robots. One or two share a striking resemblance to the film’s automated sentry guns, which guard an entrance passage in the colony. But drone aircraft, in heavy use today, are notable by their absence.
However, one robot in Aliens operates at a level far beyond the rest: the android Bishop, played by Lance Henriksen. Bishop looks like a human on the outside and is referred to in the film as a “synthetic”.
By 2179, synthetics appear to be approaching human levels of cognitive function – something known as artificial general intelligence (AGI). They even seem to observe the laws of robotics devised by scientist and author Isaac Asimov. In one scene, Bishop tells crew members that he cannot harm a human or allow one to be harmed – Asimov’s first law.
Synthetics occupy capable and realistic bodies which seem to incorporate soft robotics. In this real research area, scientists create robots with flexible materials instead of hard ones, such as metal. Fluids or pressurised air generate movement rather than conventional electric actuators.
The synthetics probably have soft robotic systems overlaid on a rigid framework, similar to flesh on bone. They are therefore likely to be a mixture of soft and conventional robotics.
Tech conundrum
Some of the tech in Aliens remains well out of reach. We don’t have propulsion systems capable of sending crews to other stars and back within a lifetime. As regards hypersleep, in rare cases, humans have survived extreme hypothermia for over an hour, but this is not recommended. Terraforming, meanwhile, remains resolutely theoretical. But what of the synthetics?
Rightly or wrongly, many researchers and companies aspire to create humanoid robots and achieve AGI. We are bombarded with visions of their latest efforts on social media. But some proportion of those working on such ventures are looking to raise money. Many experts would argue that synthetic humans like those in the Alien movies are still far beyond today’s capabilities.
This leads us to a striking conundrum at the heart of Aliens. Why aren’t there more synthetics? Why not send a population of them to terraform worlds or fight aggressive ETs?
Perhaps humans are more expendable: maybe we will end up doing AI’s dirty work because we are the cheaper commodity. But there is a more optimistic answer. Maybe, despite all of our apparent failings and weaknesses, humans are the more capable being.
After all, it is Ripley – not Bishop – who, wildly improvising with available technologies and driven by her unstoppable desire to protect Newt, defeats the alien queen. Perhaps there is hope yet for our species.
summary: James Cameron's 1986 film Aliens features a variety of futuristic technologies, some of which have paralleled modern advancements while others remain in science fiction. While the movie successfully predicted elements like wearable cameras, motion detectors, exoskeletons, and automated sentry guns, technologies such as interstellar travel, hypersleep, and true artificial general intelligence remain out of reach. The film's industrial aesthetic notably lacks personal electronic devices and modern surveillance networks, yet highlights the enduring capability of humans over machines.
key_points: The 1986 film Aliens turns 40 in August and depicts numerous technologies ranging from interstellar travel to exoskeletons.
Some technologies shown in the film have materialized today, including motion detectors, wearable cameras, biosensors, and exoskeletons.
Other prominent technologies from the movie, such as interstellar propulsion, hypersleep, and terraforming, remain theoretical or impossible.
The film's advanced android, Bishop, showcases features resembling artificial general intelligence and soft robotics, though human-like synthetics are still far beyond current capabilities.
Despite featuring advanced machinery and automated sentry guns, the film notably lacks modern personal electronic devices and drone aircraft.

title: Russian drone attack on busy shopping centre kills 15 in Ukraine
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![Firefighters work at the site of a shopping mall hit by Russian drone strikes in Kryvyi Rih, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine August 21, 2026. Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha via Telegram/Handout via REUTERS ATTENTION EDITORS - THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY. DO NOT OBSCURE LOGO. NO RESALES. NO ARCHIVES.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/reuters_6a8895ae-1787336110.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Russian drones have hit a busy shopping centre in the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, killing at least 15 people and wounding more than 130.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the Kryvyi Rih Defence Council, said on Telegram that Friday’s strikes targeted the city’s largest shopping complex, sparking a fire.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Ex-defence chief’s call for wartime election raises pressure on Zelenskyy
- list 2 of 3Nord Stream bombing suspect to Hollywood fixer: Who is Volodymyr Zhuravlev?
- list 3 of 3Russia says ready for ‘new ideas’ on Ukraine war that match Putin’s goals
Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that 22 children were among the wounded, five of which in serious condition. Overall, 29 people were in serious condition, he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack on his hometown as “cynical and despicable”.
He said a second Russian drone hit the shopping centre 30 minutes after the first, in what he claimed was a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.
“Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts,” Zelenskyy said on Telegram, urging the world to hold Russia to account.
“The world must respond to them accordingly – with real pressure on the aggressor. For peace to be possible, Russia must face real accountability,” he added.
Videos on social media showed rescuers rushing to help the wounded on the street outside, as smoke billowed from the building.
Meanwhile, a separate Russian strike in the Mykolaiv region killed four people, including three children, the country’s Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
![This handout photograph taken and released by the Ukrainian State Emergency Service on August 21, 2026 shows firefighters taking part in operations against a fire at the site of a shopping mall damaged following a Russian strike in Kryvyi Rih amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a8888cac750-1787332810.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
‘Blatant act of terror’
Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said the attack on the mall had sparked outrage. “Some are calling it a blatant act of terror, saying Ukraine must respond to it accordingly.”
Macalpine said it was unclear whether the mall was the intended target – as drones are at times intercepted and can fall haphazardly – but that video footage suggested the attack was deliberate.
Macalpine noted that Ukraine has been stepping up attacks in recent weeks on Russian warehouses linked to Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, drawing Moscow’s ire.
Kryvyi Rih, an industrial city that lies roughly 60km (37 miles) from the front line, has come under repeated Russian attacks throughout the war.
Russia has intensified its bombardments of Ukrainian cities in recent months. Ukraine has also stepped up its own attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow’s ability to wage war.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported that at least 437 civilians were killed and another 2,610 injured in Russian attacks in July. That is the highest monthly civilian death toll since May 2022.
Countries allied with Ukraine – the 34-member so-called “coalition of the willing” – will meet to reaffirm support for Kyiv on Monday, Ukrainian independence day.
summary: Russian drone strikes hit a busy shopping centre in the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, killing at least 15 people and injuring more than 130, including 22 children. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack as a terrorist act, stating that a second drone struck the area 30 minutes after the first to target emergency services. Additionally, a separate Russian strike in the Mykolaiv region resulted in the deaths of four people, including three children.
key_points: Russian drone strikes targeted the largest shopping complex in Kryvyi Rih, killing 15 people and wounding over 130.
Among the wounded were 22 children, with 29 people in total listed in serious condition.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that a second drone hit the shopping centre 30 minutes after the initial strike to target emergency services.
A separate Russian strike in the Mykolaiv region killed four people, including three children.

title: One killed in sword attack at Swedish school
author: Jamie Whitehead
content:
![Armed police officers at the scene of the Sweden school shooting](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/ef32/live/454712a0-9d7b-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Police respond to the scene in Fagersta
- Published
One person has been killed in a sword attack at a high school in central Sweden, authorities have said.
Police were called to the Brinell School in Fagersta shortly after 14:00 local time (13:00 BST) on Friday, where officers arrested an 18-year-old man.
In an update on Friday, police said officers fired at the suspect before arresting and detaining him. He has not been named.
Two teenage boys were seriously injured in the attack. Another person had minor injuries.
Eight other schools in the area were placed under lockdown measures - which have now been lifted - while a state of high alert was declared in the VÃ¤stmanland region following the attack.
Sweden's public broadcaster reported that the suspect was wearing a helmet. Local media also said he was a former student.
Police said officers were now working to establish possible motives, adding that there was currently no danger to the public.
In a post on X, Sweden's Prime Minsiter Ulf Kristersson described the attack as a "serious incident," and said "we do not know what lies behind the act, but we know that police are working very intensively".
Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said he received the news "with dismay and sadness".
In a statement, he said: "My thoughts are with those directly affected, as well as their families and loved ones."
Students at Brinell School had only just returned to the classroom following the summer break, with the new term beginning either on Monday or Wednesday this week, depending on the academic year.
The school has just under 500 students on its roster, according to SVT, and is located 170km (105 miles) north-west of the capital, Stockholm.
Sweden has experienced a number of attacks on educational institutions in recent years.
The country experienced its worst-ever mass shooting in 2025, where 11 people, including the gunman, died at an adult education centre in Ãrebro.
This led to the government tightening the country's gun laws after it was found that the suspect legally owned four rifles, three of which were found in the school where attack took place.
Two teachers were killed in a violent attack on a secondary school in Malmo in 2022 - an 18-year-old student later confessed to the attack.
In 2015, a teacher and a pupil were killed in a sword attack at a school in TrollhÃ¤ttan.
summary: One person was killed and multiple others were injured in a sword attack at a high school in Fagersta, central Sweden. Police responded to the Brinell School, shot and arrested an 18-year-old male suspect, and placed nearby schools under temporary lockdown. Authorities are currently investigating the motive behind the attack, which has drawn condolences from Sweden's prime minister and king.
key_points: One person was killed and three others were injured, including two teenage boys with serious injuries, in the attack at Brinell School.
Police shot and arrested an 18-year-old man at the scene.
Eight other schools in the area were temporarily placed under lockdown.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and King Carl XVI Gustaf both issued statements addressing the incident.

title: Russian double-tap strike on shopping center in Kryvyi Rih kills at least 15, injures 130
author: Tania Myronyshena
content:
Russian double-tap strike on shopping center in Kryvyi Rih kills at least 15, injures 130
